title: The Five Gospels
excerpt: Mark, Matthew, Luke, John and Thomas examined: authorship, sources, dates and discrepancies.

title: Mark, the first gospel
excerpt: Anonymous, written around 70 CE, and used by both Matthew and Luke.
body: @consensus

Mark is the shortest of the four gospels and, on the view held by most scholars since the nineteenth century, the first to be written. It runs to sixteen chapters and about eleven thousand Greek words. It has no birth story, no genealogy, no Sermon on the Mount and no Lord’s Prayer, and in the oldest manuscripts it has no appearance of the risen Jesus. It begins with John the Baptist at the Jordan and ends with three women running from an empty tomb, saying nothing to anyone, because they were afraid.
## Who wrote it

The text names no author. The title “According to Mark” was attached in the second century, when the churches needed to tell the gospels apart. The earliest claim about authorship is from Papias of Hierapolis, writing around 110 to 130 CE and quoted by Eusebius two centuries later: Mark, “the interpreter of Peter”, wrote down accurately but not in order what he remembered of Peter’s preaching (Ecclesiastical History 3.39.15). Papias did not know the author and was himself repeating what he had been told by “the elder”. Scholars treat the tradition with caution. The gospel shows no special knowledge of Peter, presents him unflatteringly, and depends on earlier oral units that had already taken fixed shape. What can be said is that the author wrote in Greek for an audience that did not know Aramaic (he translates it: 5:41; 7:34; 15:34) or Jewish custom (he explains it: 7:3-4), and that he used Latin loanwords (legion, denarius, praetorium, centurion), which has suggested Rome, though Syria is also argued.
## When

Most scholars place Mark between 65 and 75 CE. The anchor is chapter 13, where Jesus foretells the destruction of the Temple and the reader is told to understand (13:14). The Temple fell to Titus in August 70 CE. Whether the gospel was written in the shadow of that event or just after it is debated; that it was written within a few years of it is widely agreed. On this dating the author wrote some forty years after the events, in a different language from the one Jesus spoke, in a city far from Galilee, for people who had never been there.
## What kind of book it is

Mark moves fast. “Immediately” (euthys) occurs more than forty times. The Greek is plain, sometimes rough, and later writers smoothed it: where Mark has Jesus unable to do a mighty work in Nazareth (6:5), Matthew has him choose not to (13:58); where Mark’s Jesus is asked “Why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone” (10:18), Matthew rewrites the question so the problem disappears (19:17). Mark’s Jesus commands silence about his identity (1:34; 3:12; 8:30), a feature William Wrede named the messianic secret in 1901 and which scholars still debate. His disciples misunderstand him throughout, and at the end all of them flee (14:50).
## Where it ends

The two oldest complete Greek Bibles, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both of the fourth century, end the gospel at 16:8. So do the earliest Syriac and Latin witnesses, and Eusebius and Jerome both say the accurate copies ended there. Verses 16:9-20, in which the risen Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene, to two travellers and to the eleven, are found in later manuscripts. Their vocabulary and style differ from the rest of the gospel, they do not follow smoothly from verse 8, and one manuscript (Codex Washingtonianus) adds a further paragraph inside them. A different “shorter ending” also circulated. Modern critical editions print 16:9-20 in brackets, and most modern translations mark the passage as a later addition. The earliest gospel, as it has come down to us, contains no account of anyone seeing Jesus after his death.
## Mark and the law

In 7:19 the narrator adds, after a saying about what defiles a person, the words “thus he declared all foods clean”. The comment is the author’s, not Jesus’s, and Matthew, who copies the passage, leaves it out (15:17). The Jerusalem community under James went on keeping the food laws (Galatians 2:12; Acts 21:20), which they would not have done had Jesus declared them void. The verse is an early sign of how the gospel writers’ own positions shaped what they recorded.
## Why it matters here

Matthew and Luke both rework Mark, each reproducing most of it. Because the source survives, the changes they made can be seen, sentence by sentence, and they show how freely the tradition was handled within one generation of its first written form. Anything a reader wants to know about the earliest recoverable account of Jesus must begin with this book, and this book is anonymous, late, Greek, and ends without a risen Jesus. See the synoptic problem and the discrepancy tables.
## Sources
- Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39, for Papias.
- Bruce Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd ed., notes on Mark 16:9-20.
- Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament, chapter on Mark.
- Adela Yarbro Collins, Mark: A Commentary, Hermeneia.
- William Wrede, The Messianic Secret (1901; English translation 1971).

title: Matthew and the law
excerpt: Mark rewritten for a Jewish-Christian community: a genealogy, a nativity, and a law that does not pass away.
body: @consensus

Matthew is the first book of the New Testament but not the first gospel. It reproduces about ninety percent of Mark, often word for word, adds a large body of teaching that it shares with Luke, and supplies material found nowhere else: the genealogy, the magi, the flight to Egypt, the parable of the sheep and the goats, the guard at the tomb. It was written in Greek, not translated from Hebrew or Aramaic, and is usually dated between 80 and 90 CE. Its author is unknown.
## The name

Papias said that “Matthew compiled the sayings (logia) in the Hebrew dialect, and each interpreted them as he was able” (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39.16). Whatever Papias meant, it does not describe this book, which is a Greek narrative built on a Greek Mark and shows no sign of translation. An apostle who had followed Jesus would not have needed to copy his memories from someone who had not. The name Matthew was attached to the gospel in the second century; the tax collector called Levi in Mark 2:14 is renamed Matthew in this gospel (9:9), which may be where the association began.
## Setting

The gospel was written for a community of Jewish followers of Jesus in conflict with the synagogue after the fall of the Temple. It quotes the Jewish scriptures more than any other gospel, with a formula of its own: “this took place to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet” (1:22; 2:15, 17, 23; 4:14; 8:17; 12:17; 13:35; 21:4; 27:9). Several of these quotations do not match any known text of the prophet cited, and 2:23 (“he shall be called a Nazorean”) matches nothing at all. Antioch in Syria is the most common proposal for its origin.
## The genealogy and the nativity

The gospel opens with a genealogy of Jesus through Joseph, arranged in three sets of fourteen (1:1-17), though the third set contains only thirteen names. Luke also gives a genealogy through Joseph (3:23-38), and between David and Joseph the two lists share almost no names; even Joseph’s father differs (Jacob in Matthew, Heli in Luke). Both trace descent through Joseph, whom both say was not the father. Matthew’s nativity is told from Joseph’s side: a dream, the magi, Herod’s massacre, the flight to Egypt, the return to Nazareth because Judaea was unsafe (2:22), which assumes the family had lived in Bethlehem. Luke’s nativity is told from Mary’s side, has the family living in Nazareth and travelling to Bethlehem for a census, and has them return home peacefully after forty days. The two accounts agree that Jesus was born in Bethlehem of a virgin named Mary, betrothed to Joseph, in the days of Herod, and on little else. See the discrepancy tables.
## The law

Matthew 5:17-19 has Jesus say that he has come not to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfil them; that not one letter or stroke will pass from the law until heaven and earth pass away; and that whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments, and teaches others to do so, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. No other gospel has the saying. In 23:2-3 Jesus tells the crowds to do whatever the scribes and Pharisees teach, since they sit on Moses’ seat, but not to imitate their conduct. In 10:5-6 and 15:24 he limits his mission to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Matthew also removes Mark’s comment that Jesus declared all foods clean (compare Mark 7:19 with Matthew 15:17). This is the gospel of a community that kept the law and believed Jesus had told them to. It sits uneasily beside Paul of Tarsus, who wrote that Christ is the end of the law (Romans 10:4) and that no one is justified by its works (Galatians 2:16). See Paul of Tarsus against Jesus.
## Matthew’s additions

Where Matthew adds to Mark, the additions tend in one direction. Mark’s young man at the tomb becomes an angel descending in an earthquake (28:2). Mark’s silent women run to tell the disciples and meet Jesus on the way (28:8-9). A guard is posted at the tomb, and a story is told that the Jewish authorities bribed the soldiers to say the body was stolen, “and this story is still told among the Jews to this day” (28:11-15), a sentence written for readers two generations later. At the crucifixion the tombs open and many saints rise and walk into Jerusalem (27:52-53), an event no other writer, Christian or otherwise, records. The gospel ends with the eleven on a mountain in Galilee, where “some doubted” (28:17), and the command to baptise in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (28:19), the only threefold formula in the gospels; in Acts, baptism is in the name of Jesus alone (2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5).
## Why it matters here

Matthew is the gospel most used by the Jewish-Christian groups who kept the law and rejected Paul of Tarsus; Irenaeus says the Ebionites used it alone (see the Ebionites). It preserves, more than any other gospel, a Jesus who confirms the Torah, which is what the Qur’an says of him (3:50; 5:46). It also shows, more than any other, how a community wrote its own situation back into the story.
## Sources
- Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament, chapter on Matthew.
- Raymond Brown, The Birth of the Messiah, on the two infancy narratives.
- Ulrich Luz, Matthew 1-7: A Commentary, Hermeneia.
- W. D. Davies and Dale Allison, The Gospel According to Saint Matthew, International Critical Commentary.

title: Luke and his sources
excerpt: A preface that admits earlier accounts, a second nativity, and a sequel in Acts.
body: @consensus

Luke is the longest of the four gospels and the first volume of a two-volume work; the Acts of the Apostles is the second. It is the only gospel to open with a formal preface in the manner of the Greek historians (1:1-4), and the preface is the nearest thing the New Testament has to a gospel writer explaining his method. It is usually dated between 80 and 90 CE, though some scholars place it later, and its author is unknown.
## What the preface admits

“Since many have undertaken to set down an orderly account of the events that have been fulfilled among us, just as they were handed on to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word, I too decided, after investigating everything carefully from the very first, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus.” Three things follow. The author was not an eyewitness; he received the tradition from those who were. Written accounts already existed, and there were many of them, not two or three. And the author thought those accounts could be improved on, which is why he wrote. The synoptic evidence agrees: Luke takes over most of Mark and a body of sayings shared with Matthew, rearranges both, and adds a great deal of his own, including the parables of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son. See the synoptic problem.
## The name

A Luke is named three times in the letters as a companion of Paul of Tarsus (Philemon 24; Colossians 4:14; 2 Timothy 4:11), and the “we” passages of Acts (16:10-17; 20:5-15; 21:1-18; 27:1-28:16) are written in the first person plural. The second-century church put the two together. Against it, Acts and the letters disagree about Paul of Tarsus’s career at several points where a travelling companion would have known better (see Acts against Galatians), and Acts never mentions that Paul of Tarsus wrote letters at all. Most scholars treat the author as an educated Greek-speaking Christian of the second generation, writing for gentile readers, and leave his name open.
## The nativity

Luke’s infancy story is told from Mary’s side and runs parallel to the story of John the Baptist, birth for birth. It dates the birth of Jesus to a census ordered by Augustus “when Quirinius was governor of Syria” (2:2). Quirinius became governor in 6 CE, and the census he conducted, recorded by Josephus, covered Judaea, not Galilee, and did not require anyone to travel to an ancestral town. Matthew dates the birth to the reign of Herod the Great, who died in 4 BCE. The two dates are ten years apart, and no satisfactory reconciliation has been found. Luke has no magi, no massacre and no flight to Egypt; the family presents the child in the Temple after forty days and goes home to Nazareth (2:39).
## The genealogy

Luke traces Jesus through Joseph back to Adam and to God (3:23-38), seventy-seven generations, where Matthew counts forty-two from Abraham. From David to Joseph the two lists diverge: Matthew runs through Solomon, Luke through Nathan, and the names between share almost nothing but Shealtiel and Zerubbabel. Joseph’s father is Heli in Luke and Jacob in Matthew. Attempts to harmonise them, by making one the genealogy of Mary or by levirate marriage, go back to Julius Africanus in the third century and have persuaded few historians.
## The resurrection in Luke

Luke’s appearances all take place in and around Jerusalem on a single day: the road to Emmaus, the upper room, and the ascension from Bethany that evening (24:13-53). Matthew sends the disciples to Galilee, where Jesus meets them on a mountain (28:16). Mark’s young man says Jesus is going ahead to Galilee (16:7). Luke rewrites that message so that it refers back to what Jesus said while he was in Galilee (24:6), and his disciples are told to stay in the city (24:49). Acts then spreads the appearances over forty days (1:3). See the resurrection accounts compared.
## Luke and Acts

Acts is the only narrative of the first generation after Jesus, and of Paul of Tarsus’s career, apart from the letters. It gives Paul of Tarsus three speeches about his conversion that differ from one another (9:3-9; 22:6-11; 26:12-18) and a council in Jerusalem whose decree Paul of Tarsus never mentions (15:20, 29). Where Acts and the letters disagree, historians prefer the letters. Acts ends with Paul of Tarsus in Rome, preaching unhindered, and with the Jews rejecting the message and the gentiles receiving it (28:25-28). That is the author’s argument, and the gospel is written to lead up to it.
## Why it matters here

Luke tells the reader, in his own voice, that he worked from earlier documents and oral report, that he was not present, and that he arranged his material to make a point. That is an honest description of a work of history, and it is not a description of revelation. The Injīl the Qur’an speaks of was given to ʿĪsā (5:46). Luke is a book written about him, a lifetime later, by a man who says he was not there.
## Sources
- Joseph Fitzmyer, The Gospel According to Luke, Anchor Bible, two volumes.
- Raymond Brown, The Birth of the Messiah, on the census.
- Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.1-2, on the census of Quirinius.
- Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament, chapters on Luke and Acts.

title: John and the Jesus who speaks of himself
excerpt: The latest gospel, and the only one in which Jesus makes plain claims about his own nature.
body: @consensus

John is the latest of the four gospels, usually dated between 90 and 110 CE, and the most different. It shares almost no wording with the other three. Its Jesus cleanses the Temple at the start of his ministry, not the end; visits Jerusalem three times, not once; dies on the day before Passover, not on it; and speaks in long discourses about himself rather than in parables about the kingdom. It has no birth story, no baptism scene, no temptation, no exorcisms, no transfiguration, no Last Supper words over bread and wine, and no agony in Gethsemane. What it has instead is a Jesus who says who he is.
## Who wrote it

The gospel does not name its author. It ends by attributing its testimony to “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (21:24), who is never named either, and the chapter that says so is an appendix: the gospel has already ended at 20:31. Irenaeus, around 180 CE, identified the author as John the son of Zebedee, writing in Ephesus in old age. Modern scholars note that the beloved disciple appears only in the Jerusalem scenes, that the gospel’s Greek and theology are far from a Galilean fisherman’s, and that the text shows signs of more than one hand: a prologue in a different style, a farewell discourse that ends at 14:31 (“Rise, let us be on our way”) and then continues for three more chapters, and the appended chapter 21. Most speak of a Johannine community and a school rather than an author. Papyrus 52, a scrap of chapter 18 in the John Rylands Library, is the oldest known fragment of any gospel and is dated to the first half of the second century, which sets a lower limit for the book’s circulation in Egypt.
## The prologue

John 1:1-18 is a hymn to the Word (Logos), who was in the beginning with God and was God, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh. It is the clearest statement of pre-existence in the four gospels. Nothing like it is in Mark, the earliest, whose Jesus becomes Son of God at his baptism (1:11), or in Matthew and Luke, whose Jesus is so from his conception. The doctrine developed, and the order of the gospels shows it developing. In 1:18 the manuscripts disagree over whether the one who has made God known is “the only Son” or “the only God”; the oldest papyri have the second, and editors are divided.
## The Jesus who speaks of himself

Only in John does Jesus say “I am the bread of life” (6:35), “the light of the world” (8:12), “the resurrection and the life” (11:25), “the way, the truth and the life” (14:6), “before Abraham was, I am” (8:58), and “the Father and I are one” (10:30). Only in John does Thomas address him as “my Lord and my God” (20:28). These sayings are the foundation of the Christian doctrine of the incarnation. They are absent from the three earlier gospels, which record the same ministry. If Jesus had said such things, in public, to the crowds and to the authorities, it is hard to explain why Mark, Matthew and Luke left every one of them out. Most critical scholars conclude that the discourses are the community’s reflection on Jesus, placed in his mouth, rather than his words.
## Two voices in one gospel

The same gospel preserves sayings that point the other way, and they are as plain as the others. “The Father is greater than I” (14:28). “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (17:3). “I can do nothing on my own” (5:30). “My teaching is not mine but his who sent me” (7:16). “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (20:17). When the Jews accuse him of making himself God, he answers from Psalm 82 that scripture calls men gods, and claims for himself only the title Son of God, as one whom the Father sanctified and sent (10:33-36). Christian tradition reads these texts of the Son’s human nature or his obedience. The Islamic reading takes them at face value, as the Qur’an does: he said only what he was commanded, worship God, my Lord and your Lord (5:117).
## Two famous passages

The story of the woman taken in adultery (7:53-8:11) is absent from every Greek manuscript before the fifth century, from the oldest Syriac and Coptic versions, and from the commentaries of the Greek fathers; in the manuscripts that have it, it moves about, appearing after 7:36, after 21:25 and in Luke after 21:38. It is printed in brackets in modern editions. The ending of chapter 21, with its claim that the whole world could not contain the books that might be written, is part of the appendix. Neither passage belongs to the gospel as first written.
## Why it matters here

John is the gospel on which the claim that Jesus taught his own divinity rests, and it is the latest, the most theological, and the furthest from the words of the other three. The Qur’an’s portrait of ʿĪsā, a servant and messenger who called men to worship God alone, agrees with the earlier gospels and with the second voice in John. The measure applied on this website keeps that voice and sets the other aside, and says so. See the measure and Paul of Tarsus against Jesus, where the doctrine is traced to its other source.
@islamic

Al-Fārūqī reads the same sayings from the Aramaic side. “Son of man” in Jesus’s world meant a human being, and the synoptics use it so; “son of God” in Hebrew usage was the king, the righteous, or Israel; Kyrios, Mār, Mārī is “master”, the address of a servant to the one who sent him; and “I and the Father are one”, if Jesus said it, is the ordinary idiom of a man whose will is wholly one with his master’s, “which can be heard even today in Arabic a hundred times a day in any village market place”. Only in John and in the letters of Paul of Tarsus does sonship become metaphysical, and the prologue’s Word that was with God and was God, together with the creed’s “begotten not made” and “light of light”, is, he argues, the vocabulary of the Gnostic emanation schools, for whom the Logos was the first intelligence proceeding from the unknowable Father. On that reading the two voices in John are a Semitic teacher and a Hellenistic editor, and the measure keeps the first (al-Fārūqī, pp. 10-16).
## Sources
- Raymond Brown, The Gospel According to John, Anchor Bible, two volumes.
- Raymond Brown, The Community of the Beloved Disciple.
- Bruce Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, on John 1:18 and 7:53-8:11.
- Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1, for the tradition of authorship.

- Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Divine Transcendence and Its Expression (Kuala Lumpur: Muslim Youth Movement of Malaysia, 1983), pp. 10-16, on the titles and sayings read in their Semitic sense and on the Gnostic source of the Logos.

title: The Gospel of Thomas
excerpt: A sayings collection with no narrative: what it is, when it was written, and where its sayings are used in this gospel.
body: @consensus

The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of 114 sayings attributed to Jesus. It has no birth story, no miracles, no arrest, no crucifixion and no resurrection. Its opening line names the writer as Didymos Judas Thomas, and the name is a claim of authority, not evidence of authorship.
## Manuscripts

The text survives complete only in Coptic, in Nag Hammadi Codex II, tractate 2, found in Egypt in 1945 and copied in the fourth or fifth century. Three Greek manuscripts from Oxyrhynchus show that the work is older than the Coptic copy: P.Oxy. 1 (late second or early third century) has most of sayings 26-30 and 77 and sayings 31-33; P.Oxy. 654 (middle or late third century) has the prologue and sayings 1-7; and P.Oxy. 655 (third century) has parts of sayings 24 and 36-39. See the manuscripts of the extracanonical gospels.
## Date and sources

Scholars date the work anywhere from the middle of the first century to the middle of the second; Peter Kirby’s survey at Early Christian Writings gives 50 to 140 CE. Ron Cameron places it between the mid-first and the late second century, and thinks a late first-century date likelier if it began as a freestanding collection of sayings. Stephen Patterson argues for about 70 to 80 CE, with the present form coming from eastern Syria, where the Judas Thomas tradition flourished. The first writer to name the work beyond doubt is Hippolytus of Rome (writing 222 to 235 CE), who quotes a variant of saying 4.

Scholars divide on whether it depends on the canonical gospels. Patterson argues that it reflects a parallel and separate tradition, as does Stevan Davies, from the different order of the sayings; Cameron holds that dependence has not been convincingly shown. A statistical test of the order of the parallel sayings finds no significant correlation with Matthew, Mark, Luke or Q; it is set out on its own page. Cameron adds that the text was unstable in transmission, since the Greek copies and the Coptic differ. About half its sayings have a parallel in Matthew, Mark or Luke. The rest are unique to Thomas, and many carry an ascetic and mystical tone that the Qur’an does not share.
@minority

A minority of scholars hold that Thomas preserves sayings older than the canonical gospels. Others, such as Nicholas Perrin, argue that it was composed from them and from a harmony of the four, the Diatessaron.
## How it is used here

The full text is on its own page, in Mark Mattison’s public-domain translation and in the Patterson and Meyer translation. Those sayings that agree with the Qur’an as the measure, and those that are beyond it or unclear, are woven into the sections of The Gospel According to Islam, each with its saying number, a colour mark and a note. 44 sayings that conflict with the Qur’an or only repeat another are listed, with the reason for each, on the page of sayings set aside.
## The colour marks
- [agree] Agrees with the Qur’an as the measure.
- [beyond] Beyond the measure: the Qur’an says nothing either way. Included, and marked.
- [unclear] Unclear: the text or its sense is uncertain. Included, and marked.
## Sources

- Thomas O. Lambdin (trans.), “The Gospel of Thomas”, in The Nag Hammadi Library in English, ed. James M. Robinson, 3rd ed. (Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1988). Saying numbers here follow this edition; the wording used in the chapters is our own digest of it.
- Mark M. Mattison (trans.), The Gospel of Thomas, public domain, gospels.net; and the manuscript information at gospels.net/manuscript. Printed in full on its own page.

- Stephen Patterson and Marvin Meyer (trans.), “The Gospel of Thomas”, in Robert J. Miller (ed.), The Complete Gospels: Annotated Scholars Version (Polebridge Press, 1992, 1994). Printed in full, with permission, on its own page.

- “Correlation Analysis” of the order of sayings in the Gospel of Thomas, a statistical note on the order of the parallel sayings, using Helmut Koester’s list of parallels; with R. McL. Wilson, Studies in the Gospel of Thomas (London: Mowbray, 1960), and Stephen J. Patterson, The Gospel of Thomas Within the Development of Early Christianity (Claremont dissertation, 1988).

- Peter Kirby, “Gospel of Thomas”, Early Christian Writings, earlychristianwritings.com/thomas.html, which summarises the manuscripts, the dating and the debate over independence, citing Ron Cameron, Stephen Patterson and Stevan Davies.
- Helmut Koester, Ancient Christian Gospels.
- Nicholas Perrin, Thomas and Tatian.

title: Sayings of Thomas set aside
excerpt: The sayings of the Gospel of Thomas that are not used in this gospel, each with the reason.
body: Every saying of the Gospel of Thomas was tested against the Qur’an as the measure (see the measure). 70 are used in The Gospel According to Islam, each with a colour mark and a note. The other 44 are listed here with the reason for each: 37 conflict with the Qur’an and 7 only repeat another saying.
## The colour marks
- [agree] Agrees with the Qur’an as the measure.
- [beyond] Beyond the measure: the Qur’an says nothing either way. Included, and marked.
- [unclear] Unclear: the text or its sense is uncertain. Included, and marked.
- [conflict] Conflicts with the Qur’an: the saying says what the Qur’an denies, or denies what it affirms. Not used.
- [notneeded] Not needed: it repeats a saying that is already used. Not used.
## A note on “Father”

Thomas often says “the Father” where Matthew says “heaven” or Mark says “God” (compare Mark 3:35 with Thomas 99, and Matthew 13:33 with Thomas 96). Where the canonical parallel makes the same point in other words, the saying is used and the note says so. A saying is set aside only when “Father” carries a claim of sonship or shared nature, which the Qur’an rejects (5:18; 19:35; 112:3). The Qur’an itself does not call God “Father”, so this is a reading and not a settled rule.
## Sayings set aside

- [conflict] Thomas 1. The one who finds what these sayings mean will not taste death. Promises that whoever finds the meaning of the sayings will not taste death. The Qur’an says every soul will taste death (3:185).

- [conflict] Thomas 2. Seekers must keep seeking. Finding brings distress, then wonder, and then rule over everything. Seeking ends in ruling over the All. Rule over all things belongs to God alone (3:26; 67:1).

- [conflict] Thomas 3. The kingdom is not in the sky or the sea. It is within and around you. Knowing yourselves is how you learn you are children of the living Father. Tells the hearers they are children of the living Father. The Qur’an rejects the claim to be God’s children (5:18).
- [notneeded] Thomas 5. See what is in front of you and the hidden will be shown. Nothing hidden stays hidden. Parallel to Mark 4:22 and Luke 8:17. It adds nothing the chapters need.

- [conflict] Thomas 6. Asked about fasting, prayer, almsgiving and diet, Jesus answers only: do not lie, and do not do what you hate. Everything hidden will be uncovered. Answers the disciples’ questions on fasting, prayer and alms with no command. The Qur’an prescribes all three (2:183; 2:43; 2:110).

- [conflict] Thomas 12. The disciples ask who will lead them after Jesus leaves. He names James the righteous, for whom heaven and earth were made. Names James as the one for whose sake heaven and earth came to be. The Qur’an says heaven and earth were created in truth, and names no person as their cause (44:38-39; 51:56).

- [conflict] Thomas 14. Fasting, prayer and almsgiving are said to bring sin, condemnation and harm. Disciples should eat what is set before them and heal the sick. What comes out of the mouth defiles. (Compare Matthew 15:11; Luke 10:8-9.) Says fasting, prayer and almsgiving bring sin, condemnation and harm. The Qur’an prescribes them (2:183; 2:43; 2:110). The closing lines on food echo Mark 7:15 and Luke 10:8-9.

- [conflict] Thomas 15. When you see one not born of woman, bow down and worship, for that one is your father. Commands worship of one “not born of woman” and calls him father. Worship is for God alone (17:23; 3:79-80).

- [conflict] Thomas 17. Jesus will give what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, no hand has touched, and no mind has imagined. Jesus speaks as the giver of what no eye has seen. The Qur’an says that gift is from God alone (32:17).

- [conflict] Thomas 19. Blessed is the one who existed before coming into being. Disciples who listen will be served by stones and will have five trees in Paradise that never lose their leaves. “Blessed is he who came into being before he came into being” implies pre-existence. The Qur’an likens ʿĪsā to Adam, created from dust (3:59).

- [conflict] Thomas 22. Infants at the breast show who enters the kingdom. Entry comes when two become one: inside and outside, above and below, male and female. Says male and female must become one “so that the male not be male nor the female female”. The Qur’an affirms both sexes as God’s creation (49:13; 53:45).

- [conflict] Thomas 28. Jesus stood in the world and appeared in flesh. He found all drunk and none thirsty, and he grieved for their blindness. When they shake off the wine they will repent. Says Jesus “appeared in flesh”, the language of pre-existence. The Qur’an calls him a messenger, born of Maryam (5:75).

- [conflict] Thomas 30. Where there are three gods they are gods. Where there are two or one, Jesus says, he is with them. “Where there are three gods, they are gods.” The Qur’an forbids saying “three” (4:171; 5:73).

- [conflict] Thomas 37. The disciples ask when Jesus will be revealed. It will be when they strip without shame, trample their clothes like children, and then see the son of the living one and have no fear. Undressing without shame in order to see “the son of the living one”. The Qur’an commands modesty (24:30-31; 7:26) and rejects divine sonship (19:35).

- [notneeded] Thomas 41. Whoever has will be given more. Whoever has nothing will lose even what little there is. (Compare Mark 4:25.) A proverb that the one who has will be given more (Mark 4:25). Not needed.

- [conflict] Thomas 43. Asked who he is, Jesus says they have become like the Jews, who love the tree and hate its fruit, or love the fruit and hate the tree. Likens the disciples to “the Jews” who love the tree and hate its fruit. The Qur’an does not judge a whole people alike (3:113). It also answers “who are you?” by rebuke.

- [conflict] Thomas 44. Blasphemy against the Father or the Son will be forgiven. Blasphemy against the holy spirit will not be forgiven on earth or in heaven. (Compare Matthew 12:31-32.) Lists Father, Son and holy spirit together. Matthew 12:31-32 and Luke 12:10 do not, and the Qur’an rejects a triad (4:171).

- [notneeded] Thomas 48. If two make peace in one house, they can tell the mountain to move and it will move. (Compare Matthew 18:19; 17:20.) Parallel to Matthew 18:19 and 17:20, and repeated in saying 106. Not needed.

- [conflict] Thomas 49. Blessed are the solitary and the chosen, who come from the kingdom and will return to it. Blesses the “solitary and elect”, who come from the kingdom and return to it. The Qur’an says monasticism was not prescribed (57:27).

- [conflict] Thomas 50. When asked where you came from, say from the light, which came into being by itself. When asked who you are, say you are its children, the chosen of the living Father. The sign of the Father in you is movement and rest. Says the elect came from the light and are children of the living Father. See 5:18. The story of origin is Thomas’s own.

- [conflict] Thomas 51. The disciples ask when the dead will rest and the new world come. Jesus says what they await has already come and they have not recognised it. Says the new world has already come and is not recognised. The Qur’an teaches that the Hour is still to come (7:187; 31:34).

- [conflict] Thomas 52. The disciples say that twenty-four prophets spoke in Israel and all spoke of Jesus. He says they ignored the living one before them and spoke only of the dead. Says the twenty-four prophets spoke “in” Jesus and calls them “the dead”. The Qur’an honours the earlier prophets and makes no distinction among them (2:136).

- [conflict] Thomas 53. Asked if circumcision is useful, Jesus says that if it were, children would be born circumcised. True circumcision is in the spirit. Treats circumcision as of the spirit only. The prophetic tradition counts circumcision among the acts of fiṭra (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Book of Dress).

- [conflict] Thomas 55. Whoever does not hate father and mother, brothers and sisters, and carry the cross, cannot be a disciple. (Compare Luke 14:26-27.) Whoever does not hate father and mother cannot be a disciple (Luke 14:26). The Qur’an commands kindness to parents (17:23-24; 31:14-15). Matthew 10:37 has the softer form.

- [conflict] Thomas 56. Whoever has understood the world has found a corpse, and the world is not worthy of such a person. Calls the world a corpse. The Qur’an calls its good things a provision and forbids only excess (28:77; 7:32).

- [conflict] Thomas 61. Two will rest on one couch and one will die and one will live. Salome asks who he is. He is the one from the undivided, and one who is whole will be filled with light but one who is divided with darkness. Salome at the couch. Jesus says “I am he who exists from the undivided”, a claim of shared nature with the Father (112:3). The text is damaged.

- [conflict] Thomas 64. A host sends his servant to invite guests to dinner. Each makes an excuse of business, a house, a wedding or a farm, so the host invites those found in the streets. Buyers and merchants will not enter the Father’s places. (Compare Luke 14:16-24.) The banquet (Luke 14:16-24). Thomas adds that “businessmen and merchants will not enter the places of my father”, which Luke does not say. The Qur’an permits trade (2:275).

- [notneeded] Thomas 72. A man asks Jesus to tell his brothers to divide the inheritance. Jesus asks who made him a divider. (Compare Luke 12:13-14.) Parallel to Luke 12:13-14. The Qur’an sets its own rules of inheritance (4:11). Not needed.
- [conflict] Thomas 75. Many stand at the door, but only the solitary will enter the bridal chamber. Only the solitary will enter the bridal chamber. See saying 49 and Qur’an 57:27.

- [conflict] Thomas 77. Jesus is the light above all and the all. Split a piece of wood and he is there, lift a stone and you find him. Jesus says he is the light above all and the All, and that he is in split wood and a lifted stone. The Qur’an reserves these to God (24:35; 57:4).
- [conflict] Thomas 80. Whoever has known the world has found the body, and the world is not worthy of such a person. As in saying 56, with the body in place of the corpse (28:77; 7:32).

- [conflict] Thomas 82. Whoever is near Jesus is near the fire, and whoever is far from him is far from the kingdom. Whoever is near Jesus is near the fire. The Qur’an makes nearness to God depend on obedience (3:31).

- [conflict] Thomas 85. Adam came from great power and wealth yet was not worthy of you, for otherwise he would not have tasted death. Says Adam came from great power yet was unworthy and so died. The Qur’an says Adam was made from clay, was forgiven, and died as all do (2:37; 3:59).

- [notneeded] Thomas 91. Asked who he is, Jesus says they can read the face of sky and earth but have not recognised the one in front of them. Asked who he is, Jesus rebukes the hearers (compare Luke 12:54-56). Not needed.
- [notneeded] Thomas 93. Do not give what is holy to dogs or throw pearls to swine. (Compare Matthew 7:6.) Parallel to Matthew 7:6. Not needed.

- [conflict] Thomas 100. Shown a gold coin and told Caesar demands taxes, Jesus says to give Caesar what is Caesar’s, God what is God’s, and to him what is his. (Compare Mark 12:13-17.) The coin and Caesar (Mark 12:13-17). Thomas adds “give me what is mine”, which sets Jesus beside God.

- [conflict] Thomas 101. Whoever does not hate father and mother as Jesus does cannot be his disciple, and whoever does not love them as he does likewise. His true mother gave him life. Hate father and mother “as I do”. See saying 55 and Qur’an 17:23.

- [conflict] Thomas 105. Whoever knows the father and the mother will be called the son of a harlot. Whoever knows the father and the mother will be called the son of a harlot. The Qur’an clears Maryam of any such charge (19:28-33; 4:156).
- [notneeded] Thomas 106. When you make the two one you become sons of man, and when you tell the mountain to move it will move. (Compare Matthew 17:20.) As in saying 48. Not needed.

- [conflict] Thomas 108. Whoever drinks from Jesus’ mouth will become like him, and what is hidden will be revealed. Whoever drinks from Jesus’ mouth will become like him, and he will become that person. The Qur’an says ʿĪsā is a man, like Adam (3:59).

- [conflict] Thomas 109. The kingdom is like a man whose field hides treasure that he does not know about. His son sells the field. The buyer finds the treasure and lends money at interest. (Compare Matthew 13:44.) The hidden treasure ends with the buyer lending at interest. The Qur’an forbids it (2:275), and Matthew 13:44 has no such ending.
- [conflict] Thomas 110. Whoever finds the world and becomes rich should renounce the world. Renounce the world. See saying 56 (28:77).

- [conflict] Thomas 111. The heavens and earth will roll up before you, and whoever lives from the living one will not see death. The world is not worthy of one who finds himself. Whoever lives from the living one will not see death. See saying 1 (3:185).

- [conflict] Thomas 114. Peter says that Mary should leave because women are not worthy of life. Jesus says he will lead her so she may become male, for every woman who makes herself male will enter the kingdom of heaven. Says Mary must be made male to enter the kingdom. The Qur’an honours Maryam as chosen above the women of the worlds (3:42).
## Source and credit
- Thomas O. Lambdin (trans.), “The Gospel of Thomas”, in The Nag Hammadi Library in English, ed. James M. Robinson, 3rd ed. (Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1988). The summaries above are our own wording.

title: The synoptic problem
excerpt: Why Matthew, Mark and Luke share whole sentences, and what Markan priority and Q explain.
body: @consensus

Matthew, Mark and Luke tell the same story in the same order, in many places in the same words, and sometimes with the same rare Greek expressions and the same parenthetical asides (“let the reader understand”: Mark 13:14; Matthew 24:15). Independent accounts of the same events, written in different places by different people, do not do this. Some literary relationship exists between the three. The question of what it is, and which way it runs, is the synoptic problem, and it has been studied without a break since the eighteenth century.
## The data

About ninety percent of Mark is in Matthew and about half of it is in Luke, usually in Mark’s order. Where Matthew and Luke both follow Mark, they agree with each other; where one departs from Mark’s order, the other almost always keeps it. A further two hundred and thirty or so verses, chiefly sayings (the Lord’s Prayer, the Beatitudes, the temptation story, John the Baptist’s preaching), are shared by Matthew and Luke but absent from Mark; this is called the double tradition. Each of Matthew and Luke then has material of its own: Matthew’s magi, Luke’s shepherds; Matthew’s sheep and goats, Luke’s prodigal son.
## Markan priority

Karl Lachmann observed in 1835 that Matthew and Luke agree in order only where they agree with Mark, and the conclusion that Mark is the middle term, used by both, has held the field since Heinrich Julius Holtzmann set it out in 1863. The supporting arguments are cumulative. Mark’s Greek is rougher, and it is easier to see Matthew and Luke polishing it than Mark roughening theirs. Mark’s hard sayings are softened by the other two, not the reverse: Jesus “could do no deed of power” in Nazareth (Mark 6:5) becomes “did not do many” (Matthew 13:58); “Why do you call me good?” (Mark 10:18) becomes “Why do you ask me about what is good?” (Matthew 19:17); Mark’s Jesus does not know the day or the hour (13:32), and some manuscripts of Matthew drop the words “nor the Son”. Matthew and Luke each add what Mark lacks, a birth story and resurrection appearances, and add different ones. An abbreviator who had Matthew and Luke in front of him and left out the Lord’s Prayer and the resurrection appearances is harder to imagine than two editors who supplied them.

If Matthew and Luke each used Mark, the double tradition needs a source too, since neither seems to have known the other’s special material or the other’s order for the shared sayings. Christian Hermann Weisse proposed in 1838 that they drew on a lost collection of sayings; it has been called Q, from German Quelle, since the 1890s. The Gospel of Thomas, found at Nag Hammadi in 1945, showed that a gospel consisting only of sayings was a real literary form (see the Gospel of Thomas). No copy of Q survives, and its wording is reconstructed from the places where Matthew and Luke agree. B. H. Streeter’s four-source hypothesis of 1924 (Mark, Q, M and L) remains the standard textbook account.

Q is reconstructed by comparing Matthew and Luke, and is numbered by Luke’s verses. In the reconstruction in The Critical Edition of Q, which is the base of Mark M. Mattison’s public-domain translation at gospels.net, it holds the preaching of John the Baptist and the temptation (Q 3-4), the beatitudes and the love of enemies (Q 6), the centurion’s servant (Q 7), the instructions for the mission (Q 10), the Lord’s Prayer and “ask, seek, knock” (Q 11), the woes on the Pharisees (Q 11), the sayings on anxiety (Q 12), the mustard seed and the yeast (Q 13), the great dinner (Q 14), the lost sheep (Q 15) and the coming of the Son of Humanity (Q 17). It is almost all sayings, with little story. The Gospel of Thomas is also a collection of sayings, and about half of its sayings have parallels in the gospels, which is one reason Thomas and Q are often read together.
@minority

A minority of scholars reject Q. The Farrer hypothesis, developed by Austin Farrer, Michael Goulder and Mark Goodacre, holds that Luke used Matthew as well as Mark, which accounts for the double tradition without a lost document and explains the “minor agreements” where Matthew and Luke agree against Mark in Markan passages. The older Griesbach or Two-Gospel hypothesis, revived by William Farmer, holds that Matthew was first, that Luke used Matthew, and that Mark abbreviated both. A few scholars still defend the independence of the three, but almost none who work on the texts themselves.
## What every solution has in common

On any of these solutions, the synoptic gospels are not three independent eyewitness reports that happen to agree. They are edited works in a chain of dependence, each writer copying, correcting, rearranging and supplementing the one before. Where they agree, the agreement counts once, not three times, because it is copying. Where they disagree, the disagreement is a window on what the second writer thought the first had got wrong. The “fourfold witness” of Christian apologetics is, on the gospels’ own evidence, a single tradition in several editions.
## Why it matters here

The Islamic Dilemma assumes that the gospels are a fixed and unified body of testimony that the Qur’an must either accept whole or reject whole. The synoptic problem shows the opposite. The gospels were revised in the act of being written, by their own authors, within a generation. A revelation given to ʿĪsā could lie within such books; it could not be identical with them. That is what the measure on this website is for. See the measure and The Islamic Dilemma, answered.
## Sources
- Mark Goodacre, The Synoptic Problem: A Way Through the Maze.
- B. H. Streeter, The Four Gospels: A Study of Origins (1924).
- Bart Ehrman, The New Testament: A Historical Introduction to the Early Christian Writings, chapters on the synoptic problem.
- E. P. Sanders and Margaret Davies, Studying the Synoptic Gospels.

- James M. Robinson, Paul Hoffmann and John S. Kloppenborg (eds.), The Critical Edition of Q (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2000), and Mark M. Mattison’s public-domain translation of Q at gospels.net/quelle.

title: The discrepancy tables
excerpt: Genealogies, nativity, Last Supper, crucifixion and resurrection, set side by side with references.
body: @consensus

The four gospels disagree with one another at many points, in matters large and small. That they do is not a Muslim claim; it is in every critical introduction to the New Testament and in the footnotes of every study Bible. What a reader needs is to see the texts side by side, with chapter and verse, so that the disagreement can be checked rather than asserted. That is what the tables on this website do. Each sets the four accounts in parallel columns, records only what the texts say, and keeps interpretation apart from the table. The Gospel of Thomas has a column too; it is a sayings collection with no narrative, so it is empty wherever the others tell a story, and the table says so. A table that changes an existing page is announced in the corrections log.
## The tables
- The genealogies: Matthew 1 and Luke 3 give different fathers for Joseph and different lines from David. Mark and John give none.
- The birth of Jesus: the visitors, the journey, Herod and Egypt in Matthew and Luke, and the gospels that have no birth story.
- The last supper: whether it was a Passover meal, the words over bread and cup, and what John tells instead.
- The crucifixion: the day, the hour, who carries the cross, the last words and the women.
- The resurrection accounts: who goes to the tomb, when, what they find, who speaks to them, what they are told, what they do, and where Jesus appears.
## The five areas

The resurrection table was the first because the resurrection is the claim on which the Christian reading of Jesus rests, and because the disagreements there are the hardest to reconcile. The other four areas are set out in brief below, with references, and each now has its own table.
### The genealogies

Matthew 1:1-17 traces Jesus from Abraham to Joseph in forty-two generations arranged as three fourteens; Luke 3:23-38 traces him from Joseph back to Adam in seventy-seven. From David to Joseph the lines run through different sons of David (Solomon in Matthew, Nathan in Luke), share only Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, and arrive at different fathers for Joseph (Jacob in Matthew, Heli in Luke). Both trace descent through Joseph while stating that Joseph was not the father. The usual harmonisations, that one list is Mary’s or that a levirate marriage joined two lines, are not in the texts and were first proposed in the third century.
### The nativity

Matthew sets the birth in the reign of Herod the Great, who died in 4 BCE (2:1); Luke sets it at the census of Quirinius, who became governor of Syria in 6 CE (2:2). In Matthew the family lives in Bethlehem, flees to Egypt, and settles in Nazareth only because Judaea is unsafe (2:22-23); in Luke the family lives in Nazareth, travels to Bethlehem for the census, and returns home after the presentation in the Temple (2:39). Matthew has magi, a star and a massacre; Luke has shepherds, a manger and angels. Neither mentions the other’s events, and the two itineraries cannot both be followed.
### The Last Supper

In Mark, Matthew and Luke the Last Supper is the Passover meal, eaten on the evening of 15 Nisan (Mark 14:12-16). In John, Jesus dies on the afternoon of 14 Nisan, while the lambs are being slaughtered for a Passover that has not yet been eaten (18:28; 19:14, 31), and the meal of chapter 13 is “before the festival of the Passover” (13:1). John has no words over bread and wine; he has a foot-washing instead. The date of the crucifixion therefore differs by a day between the synoptics and John, and the difference has been argued over since the second century.
### The crucifixion

Mark has Jesus crucified at the third hour, nine in the morning (15:25); John has Pilate still passing sentence at the sixth hour, noon (19:14). Mark and Matthew record one saying from the cross, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34; Matthew 27:46); Luke replaces it with “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (23:46) and adds two others; John has three sayings of his own, none of them shared with the synoptics. In Mark both criminals mock Jesus (15:32); in Luke one defends him (23:40-43). Simon of Cyrene carries the cross in the synoptics (Mark 15:21); in John Jesus carries it himself (19:17). Matthew alone has an earthquake and the dead rising from their tombs (27:51-53).
### The resurrection

The women who go to the tomb are three in Mark, two in Matthew, several in Luke and one in John. They find a young man (Mark), an angel who descends in an earthquake (Matthew), two men (Luke) or, later, two angels (John). They are told to send the disciples to Galilee (Mark, Matthew) or reminded of what Jesus said in Galilee and told to stay in Jerusalem (Luke). They say nothing to anyone (Mark 16:8) or run to tell the disciples (Matthew, Luke, John). Jesus appears first in Galilee (Matthew), in Jerusalem and Emmaus on the same day (Luke), in Jerusalem and then at the Sea of Tiberias (John), or, in the oldest text of Mark, not at all. The full table is on its own page.
## How to read the tables

Each cell gives the text in brief with its reference, in chapter:verse form. A cell that says “None” means the gospel has no such passage. “No account” in the Thomas column means that Thomas, which contains sayings and almost no story, does not tell it.

A discrepancy is not the same as an error, and a table is not an argument. Two of the differences above may be no more than two witnesses noticing different things. But a reader who has been told that the gospels are four independent and consistent testimonies should see for himself that they are not, before deciding what to make of the Qur’an’s statement that they are confirmed in part and corrected in part. The measure this website uses is stated on the measure; the tables are the evidence it works on.
## Related
- The synoptic problem: why Matthew, Mark and Luke share whole sentences.
- The Gospel of Thomas and its full text.
- The measure: the rule this website applies to every claim.
## Sources
- Raymond Brown, The Birth of the Messiah, on the genealogies and the two nativities.
- Raymond Brown, The Death of the Messiah, two volumes, on the passion narratives.
- Bart Ehrman, Jesus, Interrupted, chapter 2, for a plain-language survey of the discrepancies.
- Joachim Jeremias, The Eucharistic Words of Jesus, on the date of the Last Supper.
